Now there are other Christians who think that this out-
look stands in irreconcilable opposition to the Christian
faith and who deny that those who hold it can be called
Christians at all. And there are others again who find the
contradiction oppressive which exists between their scientific
convictions and the principles which guide them in their
daily lives, on the one hand, and on the other the miracle
stories of the New Testament; who would by all means like
to adhere to the Christian faith, but who suppose a Christian
is obliged to consider these stories to be true. Since they
cannot do that, they fall into doubt as to whether they may
still legitimately claim to be Christians in any sense.
What are we to say to all this? In the first place, that
belief in the miracle stories of the New Testament is not in
fact the essence of Christian faith. Christian faith means
rather faith in the grace of God which has been manifested
in Christ. As Luther has already said, the real work of Christ
consists in His victory over the law and over death. And to
believe in Christ means to believe in Him as the One who
frees us from the tyranny of the law and from the reign of
death; but it does not mean considering the miracle stories
of the New Testament to be true.
And what are we to say to those who retort: No! Belief
in the miracles of the New Testament is also an integral part
of the Christian faith. It is just in such assent to the truth of
these stories that Christian faith is evidenced. For Christian
faith means surrendering not only one's self-will but also
the whole domain of one's thinking; it means not setting up
one's own thoughts against the authority of God's word.
If in the life of faith we are called to sacrifice to God all that
we are and have, we must also sacrifice to Him our life on
the intellectual plane. And if these miraculous happenings
are impossible according to the mode of our present-day
thinking, then the latter is simply false and must be given up.
